topic: 1 Peter 2:9; the faithful as a priestly people; the manner of participating in the Eucharistic sacrifice

originalOcrWitnesses.sourceTextContext: The first epistle (ii. 9), 'a kingly priesthood'; distinguished from granting every faithful person the priesthood in the Reformation sense; stresses attention, prayer and co-offering in union with Christ.
The Orate fratres invites the faithful to share the sacrifice in intention; St Peter calls Christians a kingly priesthood (1 Pet. ii. 9).
originalOcrWitnesses.printedPage: approximately 147–149; original scan not visually confirmed

scripturalWitness.claim: Scripture describes baptized believers as a royal priesthood, not an indiscriminate grant of sacred Orders.

doctrinalSourceChronology.author: Pius XII
claims: The faithful are indeed said to offer Christ's sacrifice, but not by exercising sacerdotal power of the ordained celebrant.
Only the priest, representing Christ sacramentally, effects the unbloody immolation at the Consecration.
The faithful offer through the priest's hands, join the intentions of his offering, and offer themselves spiritually in union with Christ.
The Orate fratres, Memento and other plural prayers witness that ecclesial offering is not a private priest-only intention.

doctrinalSourceChronology.author: Second Vatican Council
claims: The common priesthood of all the baptized and the ministerial priesthood differ essentially, not merely in degree.
They are mutually ordered and share in the one priesthood of Christ in distinct modes.
The ordained priest makes present and offers the Eucharistic sacrifice in Christ's person; the baptized join its offering through their royal priesthood.

doctrinalSourceChronology.author: Second Vatican Council
claims: The faithful should not behave as strangers or mere passive spectators.
They are urged to offer the Immaculate Victim through the hands of the priest and with him, and to learn to offer themselves.
This description concerns participation, not a claim that the congregation pronounces the Eucharistic Consecration.

bilingualResearchDraft.english: Saint Peter calls the baptized a royal priesthood. They therefore join the Church's sacrificial offering not by possessing the priest's power to consecrate, but by uniting their intentions, prayer, thanksgiving and the offering of their own lives to Christ, the principal High Priest. Pius XII taught these distinctions before the Council; Vatican II reaffirmed the essential difference between the priesthood of the baptized and that of the ordained priest, while calling the faithful to conscious and devout participation. During Orate fratres the celebrant's words 'my sacrifice and yours' make this shared, yet unequal, participation especially clear.
bilingualResearchDraft.french: Saint Pierre appelle les baptisés un sacerdoce royal. Ils participent donc à l'offrande de l'Église non parce qu'ils auraient le pouvoir sacerdotal de consacrer, mais en unissant leur prière, leurs intentions, leur action de grâces et leur vie au Christ, souverain Prêtre. Pie XII enseignait déjà cette distinction avant le Concile. Vatican II a rappelé que le sacerdoce commun et le sacerdoce ministériel diffèrent essentiellement, tout en demandant une participation consciente et fervente des fidèles. À l'Orate fratres, la formule « mon sacrifice, qui est aussi le vôtre » exprime particulièrement cette union des fidèles à l'oblation du prêtre.

criticalComparison.agreement: Both the 1947 preconciliar encyclical and Vatican II clearly affirm meaningful participation by baptized faithful while reserving the sacramental priestly action to the ordained minister.
criticalComparison.differenceOfEmphasis: Lumen gentium provides an explicit systematic articulation of common versus ministerial priesthood; Sacrosanctum Concilium places greater stress on intelligible, active participation. These do not nullify Pius XII's doctrinal distinction.
